ai.glance: Napoleon crowns Josephine empress in Notre-Dame cathedral-a massive propaganda painting capturing the moment he took power from the Pope's hands and placed it on his own head.

story.receipt: One of the largest paintings in the Louvre at 621 x 979 cm-nearly 10 meters wide.
story.surface_layer: Inside the vast Gothic interior of Notre-Dame, Napoleon stands in imperial robes of crimson velvet and ermine, holding a golden crown aloft. Kneeling before him in white satin and diamonds, Josephine bows her head to receive it. Behind Napoleon, Pope Pius VII sits passively, hand raised in blessing. The scene is crowded with over 150 figures in ceremonial dress: marshals in gold-embroidered uniforms, ladies-in-waiting in white, clergy in vestments, and family members in the galleries above. Candelabras illuminate the scene against deep shadows.
story.type_aesthetic: Neoclassical History Painting at monumental scale. Every face is a portrait (David sketched 150 attendees). Deliberate departures from fact: Napoleon's mother appears though she boycotted the event.
story.core_philosophy: Art as state propaganda. David served the Revolution, then Napoleon, using his brush as a political weapon. The painting creates the event it claims to document.
story.cultural_context: Napoleon commissioned this to legitimize his rule. The actual ceremony (December 2, 1804) saw Napoleon crown himself, taking the crown from Pope Pius VII. David chose to depict him crowning Josephine-more visually dramatic and less provocative.

observation_details.detail: Find Napoleon's mother Letizia in the upper gallery, seated in honor. She actually boycotted the ceremony-David painted her in at Napoleon's request to rewrite history.
Every face is an individual portrait. David conducted 150 separate sittings. Look for Napoleon's sisters and marshals-each rendered with documentary precision.
Note the Pope's passive posture-hand raised but not crowning. Napoleon has already crowned himself; the Pope merely witnesses. A profound statement of secular power over religious authority.
The golden light falls on Napoleon and Josephine while the Pope recedes into shadow. David uses light as political commentary-the future belongs to the Emperor, not the Church.

deep_dive.themes: Napoleon bypassed church authority by crowning himself. The painting diplomatically shows him crowning Josephine, but everyone knew what really happened.
deep_dive.overview: David was Napoleon's official painter. This took three years to complete (1805-1807). A near-identical replica hangs at Versailles.
deep_dive.production: David arranged 150 sittings for individual portraits. Napoleon visited the studio and reportedly said: 'David, I salute you.' The Pope's passive presence was diplomatically controversial.

expert.translation: Even the emperor bowed to his image-maker.

passerby.quote: It's not a painting of what happened-it's a painting of what Napoleon wanted you to believe happened.
